concepts.title: Rate of Change of the Circle Area
concepts.definition: Differentiating the circle area expression with respect to the radius gives how fast the area grows per unit of radius, and substituting a radius value fixes that rate at that instant.
concepts.key_idea: The derivative of pi r squared is two pi r.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh106.txt example 1 and exercise 6.1 Q1, Q17 (lines ~69-93, 333-340, 405-410)
question_patterns: find the rate of change of the area of a circle with respect to its radius at the given radius
how fast does the area of a circle grow per unit radius at the given radius
evaluate dA by dr for the circle at the supplied radius
calculate the area rate of the circle when the radius is given
what is the derivative of the circle area formula at the given radius
determine how much extra area a circle gains per extra unit of radius

solution_steps.action: Differentiate pi r squared with respect to r
solution_steps.explain: The power rule gives two times pi times r.

concepts.title: Related Rates by the Chain Rule
concepts.definition: When two varying quantities both depend on time, their rates connect through the chain rule: the rate of one equals its rate with respect to the other multiplied by the other's rate with respect to time, which solves balloon, ladder, ripple and shadow problems.
concepts.key_idea: Link the unknown rate to the given rate through a shared formula.

concepts.title: Marginal Revenue of a Quadratic Revenue Function
concepts.definition: Marginal revenue is the derivative of total revenue with respect to units sold; for a revenue of the form a x squared plus b x plus c it works out to twice the quadratic coefficient times x plus the linear coefficient.
concepts.key_idea: Differentiate the revenue polynomial and substitute the sales level.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh106.txt example 6 and exercise 6.1 Q16, Q18 (lines ~315-332, 399-403, 415-422)
question_patterns: find the marginal revenue when the given number of units are sold

solution_steps.explain: a x squared gives 2 a x and b x gives b.

concepts.title: Marginal Cost of a Cubic Cost Function
concepts.definition: Marginal cost is the instantaneous rate of change of total cost with output; for a cubic cost polynomial a x cubed plus b x squared plus c x plus d it equals three a x squared plus two b x plus c evaluated at the production level.
concepts.formula: marginal_cost = 3 * cost_a * x ** 2 + 2 * cost_b * x + cost_c
concepts.key_idea: Differentiate the cost polynomial term by term, then plug in the output.
question_patterns: find the marginal cost when the given number of units are produced
what is the marginal cost for the cubic cost function at the given output level
calculate the rate of change of total cost at the given production
determine the approximate cost of one extra item at the given output
differentiate the cost function and evaluate at the supplied production level

solution_steps.explain: Each term's power drops by one with its coefficient multiplied by the old power.
solution_steps.compute: marginal_cost = 3 * cost_a * x ** 2 + 2 * cost_b * x + cost_c

concepts.title: Increasing and Decreasing Intervals
concepts.definition: A function climbs where its derivative stays positive and falls where it stays negative; to sort the real line, solve derivative equals zero, then test the sign of the derivative inside each gap between consecutive roots.
concepts.formula: f increasing on an interval when f_prime(x) > 0 there
concepts.key_idea: Roots of the derivative split the line; signs of the derivative decide the trend.

solution_steps.explain: Compute f_prime(x).
The roots cut the domain into disjoint intervals.

solution_steps.action: Test the sign in each interval
solution_steps.explain: Positive derivative marks increasing stretches, negative marks decreasing ones.

concepts.title: Critical Points of a Function
concepts.definition: A critical point is an interior domain point where the derivative vanishes or fails to exist; every local peak or valley must sit at one, though a vanishing derivative alone does not promise a peak or valley.
concepts.formula: c is critical when f_prime(c) = 0 or f_prime(c) does not exist
concepts.key_idea: Turns can only happen where the derivative is zero or undefined.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh106.txt note after theorem 2 with the x cubed remark (lines ~1397-1412)

solution_steps.explain: Compute f_prime(x).
These stationary points form one class of critical points.
Corners and cusps are critical too, even without a vanishing derivative.

concepts.title: First Derivative Test for Local Extrema
concepts.definition: At a critical point, watch the sign of the derivative on both sides: positive flipping to negative marks a local maximum, negative flipping to positive marks a local minimum, and no flip marks a point of inflexion.
concepts.formula: sign change of f_prime from plus to minus at c gives a local maximum
concepts.key_idea: The side-wise sign flip of the derivative classifies the critical point.

solution_steps.action: Probe the sign just left and just right
solution_steps.explain: Substitute nearby test values into f_prime.
Plus to minus is a local maximum; minus to plus a local minimum; no flip an inflexion.

concepts.title: Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema
concepts.definition: At a stationary point, a negative second derivative signals a local maximum and a positive one a local minimum; when the second derivative is also zero the test is silent and the first derivative test must decide.
concepts.formula: c is a local minimum when f_prime(c) = 0 and f_double_prime(c) > 0
concepts.key_idea: Concavity at the stationary point settles maximum versus minimum.

concepts.title: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
concepts.definition: On a closed interval a continuous function always attains a greatest and a least value; compare the function values at the critical points inside the interval and at the two endpoints, and pick the largest and smallest of them.
concepts.formula: absolute extrema come from comparing f at critical points and endpoints
concepts.key_idea: Endpoints join the candidate list for global highest and lowest values.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh106.txt section 6.4.1 working rule with examples 27-28 (lines ~2114-2312)

concepts.title: Max-Min Word Problems
concepts.definition: Turn an optimisation story into a single-variable function, differentiate, set the derivative to zero, and use a derivative test to certify the answer; typical targets are largest volume, least surface, maximum profit or a minimum sum of squares.
concepts.formula: optimise by solving f_prime(x) = 0 and testing the sign of f_double_prime
concepts.key_idea: Model, differentiate, solve, then certify with a derivative test.
